Separately, Iranian state media reported that a U.S.-Israeli strike targeted several petrochemical facilities in Khuzestan province; the strikes killed at least 5 and injured 170 others (Anadolu Agency). Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the strikes in a video statement, further adding that Israel will continue to strike Iran (Times of Israel). Airstrikes hit the vicinity of an Iranian nuclear power plant Saturday, prompting a worker evacuation and a warning from the UN nuclear watchdog against targeting the site (Times of Israel; UN). Retaliatory attacks continued as medics stated that at least four people were injured because of a ballistic missile attack on central Israel (Times of Israel). In the Gulf, the United Arab Emirates intercepted fifty-six drones and twenty-three ballistic missiles; Kuwait also reported nineteen drone and six missile attacks (NYT). A local channel of Iranian state television reported that a U.S. pilot ejected from their aircraft over southwestern Iran, noting that those who capture or hand in any pilots to the police would be rewarded (AP). Israel, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, and Saudi Arabia continued to report drone and missile attacks (NPR). Kuwait reported damage to a power and desalination plant, while a drone set several units at Kuwait’s Mina al-Ahmadi refinery on fire; in Abu Dhabi, falling debris from drone interception caused a fire at its Habshan gas facility (NYT). Iran’s Revolutionary Guards blamed Israel for attacking the Kuwaiti power and desalination facilities (WANA). Meanwhile, the Israeli military reported that a man was injured by debris after a missile struck northern Israel (NYT). Iran struck a defiant tone despite weathering two high-profile attacks after President Donald Trump’s prime-time address earlier this week; a U.S. airstrike on Iran’s largest bridge killed eight people, Iranian state media reported (Times of Israel). Trump touted the bombing on social media and threatened more attacks on bridges and power plants (Truth Social). An airstrike amid U.S. and Israeli bombings also destroyed one of the country’s preeminent public health establishments (The National). More than a month into the war, unnamed sources told CNN that U.S. intelligence suggests around half of Iran’s missile launchers remain intact (CNN). Meanwhile, Iran’s mission to the United Nations rebuked Trump’s Wednesday speech as a show of “ignorance, not strength” (Iranian Mission UN). The United Kingdom hosted a virtual meeting involving some thirty-five countries to discuss reopening the Strait of Hormuz (Reuters). At the UN Security Council, China, France, and Russia objected to draft resolution language that would authorize the use of military force to reopen the Strait of Hormuz; a vote is expected in the coming days (NYT). Meanwhile, Iran and Oman are preparing a framework to monitor transit through the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported (CNBC). For now, ships passing through the strait have done so via negotiations with Tehran; the Philippines said today it had gained permission to transit (Reuters). Bloomberg reported that some ships have been required to pay in Chinese yuan or cryptocurrency to get through (Bloomberg). Amnesty International accused Iran of child recruitment—a war crime—saying it had sought to draw children as young as twelve into its war effort (Amnesty). Separately, U.S.-based international law experts published a joint letter saying the conduct of all three parties in the war—Israel, Iran, and the United States—raises concerns of “serious violations of international law,” and pointing to U.S. actions they said could amount to war crimes (Just Security). Even as the U.S. offensive presses ahead—with thousands of additional troops being deployed to the Middle East—its military leadership faces an overhaul at home; three U.S. generals were reportedly removed (AP). A Defense Department spokesperson announced the departure of General Randy A. George, the former Army Chief of Staff, without citing an explanation (Pentagon). Unnamed U.S. defense officials told multiple news outlets that generals responsible for chaplains and training were also removed (CNN). Trump said the United States plans to attack Iran “extremely hard” over the next two to three weeks in a speech last night that made little mention of diplomacy; it was his first formal address about the Iran war since its start more than a month ago (NYT). Yet Trump made no major announcements, instead reiterating recent talking points: core U.S. goals are “nearing completion,” Trump said, giving no assurances about the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and saying that other countries should “take the lead” on the matter (NYT). Iran’s military command responded by vowing to carry out “more crushing, broader, and more destructive” attacks, according to state media (France24). Global oil prices rose, and stocks tumbled in the wake of Trump’s address (Reuters). Unnamed U.S. and Iranian officials told the New York Times the two countries are exchanging messages, but have not entered formal negotiations over a truce or peace deal (NYT). While Trump wrote on social media that Tehran had requested a ceasefire, Iran denied it (Truth Social). Iran believes the United States is not serious about diplomacy, according to comments from its foreign ministry spokesperson published on state media (WSJ). Earlier in the day, Trump stated he was considering withdrawing the United States from NATO due to European members’ unwillingness to send ships to the Strait of Hormuz, which remains effectively closed (Reuters). Meanwhile, Israel announced that it had completed a wave of strikes targeting government infrastructure in Iran; Iranian state media reported explosions across Tehran early in the morning (NYT). Iran continued retaliatory strikes, conducting several ballistic missile attacks on Israel; according to the Israel Defense Forces, the missiles were intercepted (Times of Israel). The IDF also reported that it intercepted a ballistic missile in southern Israel fired by the Iran-backed Houthis (Times of Israel). Iran launched three cruise missiles at Qatar; two were intercepted, and a third struck an oil tanker (NYT). In the United Arab Emirates, a Bangladeshi national was killed after he was struck by debris from a drone interception (NYT).  The Wall Street Journal reported that the United Arab Emirates is weighing joining the war to help the United States reopen the Strait of Hormuz (WSJ). U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that U.S. bombers conducted strikes on Isfahan (NYT). Hegseth also told reporters today that negotiations with Iran are “very real” and “gaining strength” (C-SPAN). Israel struck a pharmaceutical plant in Iran, while Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it planned to attack a slew of U.S. tech companies operating in the region (NYT; IRGC). Retaliatory attacks continued across the Gulf as Iran struck a large Kuwaiti oil tanker near the coast of Dubai overnight, and the United Arab Emirates’ Defense Ministry reported intercepting drones and missiles fired by Iran; meanwhile, Israeli media also reported waves of attacks on central Israel (NPR). The war has triggered rising energy prices worldwide, including in the United States, where the average price of gasoline surpassed $4 per gallon today for the first time since 2022 (AP). U.S. President Donald Trump expressed frustration with U.S. allies who have been unwilling to take additional steps to support U.S war efforts in Iran, telling them to “go get your own oil” on Truth Social (Truth Social; AP). Trump said the United States would be done with the war in “two to three weeks,” and hinted a U.S. exit could come before the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz (C-SPAN). Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera that Tehran sought an end to the regional war rather than a ceasefire, even as military hostilities continue to escalate (Al Jazeera). Pakistan’s foreign minister visited China today for talks regarding the war (China MoFA). Beijing “commends and supports” Pakistan’s mediation effort and is ready to work toward peace, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said ahead of the visit (China MoFA). Israel and the United States launched a new wave of strikes on Tehran as U.S. President Donald Trump threatened widespread destruction of Iran’s energy plants, oil wells, Kharg Island, and potentially desalination plants if a deal to end the war is not made soon (AP; Truth Social). U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the goals of degrading Iran’s military capabilities had been largely achieved (ABC). The White House press secretary declined to confirm that fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz was a “core” objective, while the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump told aides he was willing to end the war even if the strait remained mostly closed (White House; WSJ). Iran’s foreign ministry said that a fifteen-point U.S. peace plan included “excessive, unrealistic, and irrational demands” (AP). The threats come as an airstrike struck the Tabriz Petrochemical Complex in northwestern Iran early Monday, sparking a contained fire with no reported hazardous leaks (NYT). A U.S.-Israeli strike on an orphanage west of Tehran killed at least two people, Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency reported (CNN). NATO air defenses shot down an incoming Iranian missile over Turkey for the fourth time this month, Ankara said (Turkey MoND). Iran also attacked a water desalination facility in Kuwait, killing one worker (Al Jazeera). The Houthis continued retaliatory attacks as the Israel Defense Forces stated it intercepted two drones fired from Yemen (Times of Israel). While the Iran war’s precise effects on the global economy remain uncertain, “all roads lead to higher prices and slower growth,” economists from the IMF; they flagged risks of food insecurity in low-income countries from rising food and fertilizer prices, as well as potential shortages of materials needed for chips and electric car batteries (IMF). Meanwhile, the United Nations Development Program estimated in a new report that fighting in the Middle East could cost Arab countries between $120 billion and $194 billion in lost economic output; that amounts to a regional GDP decline of between 3.7 and 6 percent (UNDP). Pakistan convened talks with Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey in Islamabad on Sunday to explore ways to end the Iran war, with discussions centering on proposals to reopen the Strait of Hormuz amid surging global oil prices (Reuters). After the meeting, Pakistan’s foreign minister announced that Islamabad was also ready to host U.S.-Iran talks, though neither side confirmed the date (Bloomberg). This comes as several hundred U.S. Special Operations forces arrived in the Middle East, joining the 2,500 Marines and 2,500 sailors who recently arrived in the region (NYT). Iran’s Parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Tehran would set U.S. troops “on fire” if a ground operation is launched, according to state media (The Hindu). U.S. President Donald Trump is reportedly considering a military operation to extract close to a thousand pounds of enriched uranium in Iran (WSJ). In an interview with the Financial Times, Trump also said that he could seize Kharg Island and “take the oil in Iran” (FT). Trump also announced that Iran agreed to release twenty cargo ships through the Strait of Hormuz starting Monday, framing it as a sign of respect and evidence of ongoing negotiations he claimed were going “extremely well”; however, outside experts say it more simply demonstrates Iran’s control over the critical waterway (NYT). Escalations continued as Al Araby, a Qatari news channel, reported that Israeli strikes hit its office in Tehran (Times of Israel). The International Atomic Energy Agency also reported that Iran’s heavy water production plant in Khondab is no longer operational following March 27 strikes (Times of Israel). Meanwhile, Iran continued retaliatory attacks, firing a series of ballistic missiles at Israel; Saudi Arabia’s defense ministry also reported intercepting ten drones (NYT). The Iranian-backed Houthis entered the war, claiming two missile attacks directed toward Israel (AP). In a statement released on Saturday, the group claimed that their ballistic missiles were targeting “sensitive” Israeli military sites, further stating that attacks would continue until all aggression from all fronts comes to a halt (NYT). The Israel Defense Forces stated that air defense systems successfully intercepted both missiles (Times of Israel). The Israeli military also stated that it carried out overnight strikes in Tehran targeting weapons production infrastructure (AP). Meanwhile, Iranian state media reported that Israeli strikes struck the University of Science and Technology in northeastern Tehran; in response, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps threatened to target American universities in the Middle East  (Times of Israel). Retaliatory attacks continued across the Gulf as Bahrain, Kuwait, and the United Arab Emirates were targeted with missile and drones (AP). Two drones also struck near Oman’s port of Salalah; Iran’s military claimed it was targeting an American vessel near the port (NYT). Israel threatened to “escalate and expand” its strikes on Iran, noting that Iran needed to stop firing missiles at civilians in Israel (AP). The statement comes a day after U.S. President Donald Trump extended his deadline for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to April 7 as Iran rejected his fifteen-point proposal to end the war (Reuters). Separately, two Chinese state-owned COSCO Shipping container ships were forced to turn back in the Strait of Hormuz; the unusual move underscores the broader disruption to global shipping routes as Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has typically restricted passage to ships tied to U.S. and Israeli partners (WSJ). Meanwhile, the war continued as the Israeli military announced it conducted strikes targeting government infrastructure (NYT). The Israel Defense Forces also identified Iranian missile fire targeting central Israel (Times of Israel). The White House is reportedly still pushing for an off-ramp to the Iran war, though Iranian leaders say they are not officially negotiating; the two sides are passing indirect messages to each other via Pakistan, Pakistan’s foreign minister wrote on social media (Pakistan FM). Israel’s defense minister said its military killed the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ naval commander overnight (NYT). Pakistani officials said that Iran has received a U.S. plan to end the war, delivered as a fifteen-point proposal via Pakistan; the officials say the proposal broadly encompasses reopening the Strait of Hormuz, placing limits on missiles, sanctions relief, and a rollback on Iran’s nuclear program (AP). Unnamed U.S. officials told CNN the Trump administration is trying to set up talks in Pakistan this weekend (CNN). Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran was reviewing the fifteen-point U.S. peace plan but insisted it did not intend to negotiate (Reuters). Iranian state television quoted a senior official as saying the war would only end when Tehran’s conditions are met, including an end to fighting on “all fronts” and guarantees Iran will not be attacked in the future (FT). Trump is prepared to “unleash hell” if Tehran does not make a deal, the White House press secretary said (WSJ). U.S. defense and intelligence officials told lawmakers in a closed-door briefing that the use of ground troops had not been ruled out, without explaining what they could be used for or if they could be protected (NBC). In a sign of the tensions among Republicans over the war, Representative Nancy Mace (R-SC) wrote on social media that the briefing reaffirmed her opposition to sending U.S. troops to Iran (X). Meanwhile, Israel has accelerated strikes to hit key targets before a potential end to the war, unnamed Israeli officials told the New York Times (NYT). Retaliatory attacks also continued as Bahrain, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia reported additional missile and drone incursions, while Iran’s military announced that it fired missiles towards the U.S. aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln (NYT). Israeli media also reported smoke rising from the Rabin power plant in Hadera, Israel, after a missile barrage from Iran, though the Israel Electric Corporation stated there was no damage to its infrastructure from the attack (Anadolu Agency). Iran believes its adversaries are preparing to occupy an Iranian island with the help of a Middle Eastern country, Iran’s parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on social media; in the case of an attack, he threatened Iran would retaliate against “all the vital infrastructure” of that country (X). Israel announced that its forces were conducting continued strikes on Iran and Lebanon, while Iranian forces launched a new round of drone and missile strikes towards the Persian Gulf (WSJ). Missile fire from Iran severely damaged three buildings and lightly wounded four people at an impact site in Tel Aviv (Times of Israel). A representative for the Israeli military stated that the damage was caused by direct impact from an Iranian missile that was not intercepted (NYT). The Israeli military further revealed that the missile carried a conventional warhead rather than cluster munitions, and that the Israeli Air Force is investigating the failure to shoot down the missile (Times of Israel). In Bahrain, a civilian contractor working alongside the United Arab Emirates’ military was killed in a missile attack, and five Emirati military personnel were injured (Anadolu Agency). Meanwhile, Iran appointed Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr as the new chief of the Supreme National Security Council, replacing Ali Larijani, who was killed in an Israeli strike last week (Times of Israel). Zolghadr is a hardline former deputy commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps with experience helping the IRGC entrench itself further in Iranian politics (NYT). By the time Trump’s five-day pause on his threat to hit Iranian energy sites ends Friday, more than two thousand additional U.S. Marines are expected to arrive in the Middle East, the Wall Street Journal reported (WSJ). U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters that negotiations with Iran were continuing and that Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio will join Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in discussions (NYT). U.S President Donald Trump stated on social media that the United States and Iran held a productive conversation about ending hostilities and that he instructed the Pentagon to postpone attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure and power plants for at least five days (NYT). Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf pushed back, writing on social media that “no negotiations” were held with the United States (X). Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said that in recent days, however, “friendly states” had conveyed messages about a U.S. request for talks (FT). Egypt, Pakistan, and Turkey have reportedly spoken with both the United States and Iran in recent days (Axios). Despite this, Trump told reporters that the U.S. and Iran had productive talks that would continue today by phone, stating that his envoy, Steve Witkoff, and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, were leading the U.S. side and speaking with a “top” Iranian official (NYT). He further noted that as a part of a potential agreement with Iran, the United States would retrieve Iran’s enriched uranium (AP). Trump told reporters that if diplomacy is unsuccessful, “we’ll just keep bombing our little hearts out” (CNBC). Meanwhile, the Israeli military conducted another wave of strikes, knocking out electricity in large parts of Tehran (NYT). More than three weeks of war appear to have hardened some Gulf states’ positions toward Iran, with a senior Emirati official calling Tehran’s restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz an “act of economic terrorism” (WSJ). Iran stated that if U.S. President Donald Trump followed up on his Saturday ultimatum of striking power plants, it would completely close the Strait of Hormuz (AP). Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf, speaker of the Iranian parliament, also threatened that critical infrastructure across the region would be “irreversibly destroyed” (NBC).  Amid Trump’s ultimatum, Brent crude rose to around $114.09 a barrel, while U.S. crude rose to $100.29 (CNN). Meanwhile, U.S. and Israeli strikes continued targeting Iranian missile production and storage sites (ISW). Separately, while an ongoing internet blackout in Iran makes it difficult to determine casualties, the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency estimated that more than three thousand people have been killed in Iran since the start of the war (HRANA). Multiple U.S. officials said that Iran fired two intermediate-range ballistic missiles towards the joint U.S.-U.K. military base, Diego Garcia, in the middle of the Indian Ocean (WSJ). The semi-official Iranian news agency Mehr also reported on the event, stating that it demonstrated that Iran’s ballistic capabilities were more advanced than adversaries had previously imagined (Reuters). Neither of the missiles struck the base, as one failed, and the other was struck down by the United States; even so, the event debunked the regime’s long-standing assertion of a self-imposed two-thousand-kilometer cap on its missile capabilities (ISW). Meanwhile, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported that U.S. and Israeli strikes targeted the Natanz uranium enrichment facility, noting that no civilians were injured and that there were no reported radioactive leaks (Reuters). The Israeli military denied striking the facility, but stated it struck dozens of sites across Tehran, focusing on sites that were critical to developing ballistic missiles (NYT). Later in the day, Iranian missiles struck the Israeli towns of Arad and Dimona, injuring one hundred and eighty people (BBC). Dimona is widely believed to house Israel’s nuclear weapons program (NYT). Retaliatory attacks across the Gulf region also continued as Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates reported intercepting drones and missiles (NYT). Separately, U.S. President Donald Trump issued an ultimatum to Iran, threatening to “obliterate” Iran’s power plants if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened within forty-eight hours (AP). Axios reported that the Trump administration had begun initial conversations about peace talks with Iran, but that U.S. officials still expected two to three more weeks of fighting; an unnamed U.S. official listed six demands, including a five-year halt to Iran’s missile program, an end to financing for regional proxies, and zero uranium enrichment (Axios). Iranian state TV reported that Ali Mohammad Naini, a spokesperson and deputy of public relations for the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps, was killed in U.S. and Israeli strikes (Reuters). Israeli military officials also reported that Esmail Ahmadi, the head of intelligence for the Basij force, was killed earlier in the week (AP). Meanwhile, as the war approaches its fourth week, Israel launched more strikes in and near Tehran; Iran’s new Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, also issued a rare statement saying that Iran’s adversaries need to have their security removed (NPR). General Abolfazl Shekarchi, a spokesperson for Iran’s armed forces, additionally warned that adversaries would not be safe in “tourist centers” around the world (NBC). Retaliatory attacks on energy infrastructure continued as Kuwaiti state media reported that drone attacks caused fires at the Mina Al-Ahmadi Refinery (NYT). Amid attacks in the Gulf, Ukrainian security council secretary Rustem Umerov said that Ukraine deployed military units to Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates to protect critical and civilian infrastructure against drones (Reuters). Finally, Washington lifted sanctions on Iranian crude oil shipments loaded between March 20 and April 19 (Treasury). Iran intensified strikes across the Gulf in retaliation for the recent strike on the South Pars oil field, as natural gas facilities in Qatar were struck in Iranian strikes (AP; NYT). Qatar’s energy minister told Reuters that an Iranian strike on a major Qatari gas facility earlier this week knocked out around 17 percent of the country’s liquified natural gas export capacity (Reuters). Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud warned that tolerance for Iranian attacks in Saudi Arabia and the rest of the Gulf is limited (CNBC). As tensions increased, Brent crude prices briefly reached $119 a barrel (AP). Amid rising oil prices, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessett said the administration was considering lifting restrictions on the approximately 140 million barrels of Iranian oil already loaded onto vessels, even as the Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. attack jets and helicopters were targeting Iranian assets in the area of the Strait of Hormuz (WaPo; WSJ). U.S. President Donald Trump also said that he told Israel not to conduct additional attacks on Iranian oil infrastructure (Reuters). Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that he believes pipelines should be built to transport oil and gas through the Arabian Peninsula into Israeli ports to avoid additional Iranian threats to the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters (Reuters). Seven U.S. allies pledged to help ensure safe passage through the strait, but did not specify how they would do so (UKG). The World Trade Organization (WTO) said that if oil and gas prices remain high for the rest of the year, it could reduce the forecasted 2026 growth in global GDP by 0.3 percent; it estimated that Europe, a heavy energy importer, could see GDP grow at least one percent less than previously expected (WTO). In separate comments, U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the United States and Israel were accomplishing their battlefield goals (State). Netanyahu said that Iran no longer has the capabilities to produce ballistic missiles or enrich uranium; hours after his remarks, Iran fired a series of missiles at Israel (Times of Israel). The Israeli Army Radio reported that 85 percent of Iran’s surface-to-air missiles have been destroyed in recent strikes (ISW). Netanyahu also said Israel sought to create the conditions in Iran for a popular uprising (Times of Israel). Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on social media that any agreement to end the war must compensate Iran for the destruction of civilian sites (Iran FM). Finally, the State Department announced it had approved more than $16 billion in potential arms sales to Jordan, Kuwait, and the United Arab Emirates; all three countries have been attacked by Iran this month in the ongoing war (Reuters). Citing emergency circumstances, it waived the normal requirement for Congress to review the sales (State). Israel announced that its military killed Esmail Khatib, Iran’s intelligence minister, and that it had authorized the Israel Defense Forces to target any senior Iranian official that it can locate (Reuters). In a statement, the IDF said Khatib and his ministry oversaw covert operations against American and Israeli targets around the world (NYT). In response to Khatib’s killing, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement that it conducted a ballistic missile attack on Tel Aviv, and that the missiles penetrated Israeli air defense systems (NYT). An elderly couple was killed in the attacks, and two others were lightly wounded by shrapnel (Times of Israel). Israel attacked the Iranian portion of the world’s largest gas field, known as South Pars (AP). Iran responded by striking a liquefied natural gas facility on the Qatari side of the same gas reservoir, with the hub sustaining “extensive damage” (Qatar Energy). Kuwait and Saudi Arabia also said their energy facilities were targeted by drones (AP). The events prompted heightened warnings to Iran from Gulf countries, with Saudi Arabia threatening military retaliation and Qatar expelling senior Iranian officials from the country (Reuters; WSJ). The attacks sent jitters through markets, and the price of Brent crude oil rose above $118 per barrel before falling back below $114 (Bloomberg; FT). Trump wrote on social media that Israel would stop targeting Iran’s gas field—but threatened that if Iran attacks Qatar again, the United States would “blow up” the Iranian gas facility (Truth Social). Trump also claimed the United States “knew nothing” about the South Pars attack though multiple outlets, quoting unnamed U.S. and Israeli officials, reported he was aware and approved of the impending strike (WSJ; Axios). The Trump administration issued a sixty-day waiver yesterday allowing foreign-flagged ships to move between U.S. ports and loosened its sanctions on Venezuela’s state oil company to make it easier to sell oil directly to U.S. companies and on international markets (Guardian; FT). U.S. Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard testified at a Senate hearing that Iran’s conventional military capabilities “have largely been destroyed” but the regime appears “intact” (ODNI). In a written statement submitted prior to the hearing, she said Tehran had made “no efforts” to rebuild its nuclear enrichment capabilities after last June’s strikes (Senate Intel). In a sign that the Iran war could last considerably longer, the Pentagon asked the White House to approve a request to Congress for more than $200 billion in additional war funding, the Washington Post reported (WaPo). Israel said that it killed top Iranian security official Ali Larijani and senior military commander Gholam Reza Soleimani; Iran did not immediately confirm their deaths, which would mark the most senior Iranian figures killed since the death of former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the war’s start (CNN). As the United States faces increasing isolation from global allies in the war with Iran, top European officials said they favor diplomatic solutions to restore traffic through the Strait of Hormuz (Reuters). Countries such as France continue to resist Trump’s calls to join a military coalition to reopen the waterway (Reuters). Trump rebuked NATO, saying the alliance was “making a very foolish mistake” and that the United States did not need those allies anyway (C-SPAN). Commercial shipping through the strait remains at a trickle; Iran’s foreign minister said Saturday the waterway was only closed to “those who are attacking us and their allies,” and ships from India, Pakistan, and Turkey have sailed through since the start of the war (MS Now; Al Jazeera). Yet a Kuwait-flagged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates was struck by a projectile today (Reuters). Meanwhile, maritime tracking data showed that a ship believed to be moving Marines to the Middle East had advanced from Japan and was now close to Singapore (CNN). A top Trump administration counterterrorism official resigned over the war in Iran; former National Counterterrorism Center Director Joe Kent broke ranks with senior Trump administration officials, writing in a resignation letter that “Iran posed no imminent threat to our nation” and the war “serves no benefit to the American people” (X). Trump responded by saying that “it’s a good thing that he’s out,” calling him “very weak on security” (C-SPAN). Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard posted a statement saying the president was responsible for determining threats while intelligence officers were responsible for coordinating intelligence (DNI). Major European powers have largely rejected President Trump’s demand for naval intervention, with Germany, Italy, and Greece explicitly refusing to join military operations in the Strait of Hormuz; Germany’s defense minister said, “this is not our war” (NYT). While UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer ruled out joining a “wider war,” he signaled a willingness to work with allies on a collective plan to restore shipping, potentially using autonomous mine-hunting systems rather than warships (Reuters). Similarly, Japan’s defense minister said today that Tokyo had no plans to send ships and called for de-escalation (Bloomberg). At an event, Trump berated allies reluctant to participate in a military coalition to reopen the strait, painting them as ungrateful for years of U.S. assistance (ABC). Trump also claimed that the United States has destroyed all of Iran’s mine-laying ships as part of its efforts to reopen the strait; however, he added that Washington was unsure whether any mines had already been laid (NBC). If the crisis continues roiling global oil prices, the International Energy Agency is open to a second release of oil reserves since the start of the war, its director said (IEA). Meanwhile, Iran has asked India to release three Iran-linked tankers seized in February as part of negotiations to ensure the safe passage of Indian-flagged or India-bound vessels through the Strait of Hormuz; Tehran also requested medical equipment and certain medicines during the talks (Reuters). Separately, retaliatory attacks continued as the Israel Defense Forces detected a new ballistic missile launch from Iran (Times of Israel). Authorities in the United Arab Emirates also reported that an Iranian drone attack set a fuel tank on fire at Dubai International Airport early in the morning, as civilian infrastructure continues to be targeted across the Persian Gulf (WaPo). Trump appeared to up the pressure on allies to assist the United States in unblocking the Strait of Hormuz, telling the Financial Times that it would be “very bad for the future of NATO” if U.S. allies did not help reopen the waterway (FT). Following Iran’s retaliation pledge over U.S. strikes on Kharg Island, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) were targeted by air attacks, causing fires at a UAE port and airport (Bloomberg). Air attacks also continued across Israel, Iran, and Lebanon over the weekend (Haaretz; Iranian Red Crescent; France24). An Israeli military spokesperson told CNN that Israel planned for at least three more weeks of war (CNN). Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that Russia provided Iran with Shahed drones that were used against U.S. bases (The Hill). Iran urged citizens to evacuate the Jebel Ali port in Dubai, the Khalifa port in Abu Dhabi, and a port in Fujairah following U.S. strikes on Kharg Island on Friday; this came as Iran said that the United States had used infrastructure in the United Arab Emirates to launch Friday’s attacks (AP). U.S. forces had struck military targets on the island, which is a hub for 90 percent of Iran’s oil exports; the island was viewed as a key vulnerability that would provoke a significant response from Iran if attacked (Reuters). Iran continued retaliatory strikes across the Gulf region, as Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates reported missile and drone attacks (Al Jazeera). Separately, sources familiar with the matter reported that U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has declined attempts by U.S. allies in the Middle East to begin diplomatic efforts to end the war; Iran has also rejected a ceasefire until U.S. and Israeli strikes come to a halt (Reuters). Trump told NBC News that Iran was ready to end the war, which Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has denied (NBC News). As the Iran war enters its third week, Trump has intensified calls for allies to help unblock the Strait of Hormuz to mitigate the war’s economic impacts; in a social media post, Trump said that he hoped countries including China, France, Japan, South Korea, and the United Kingdom (UK) would send forces to secure shipping through the strait (Truth Social). After a drone struck the U.S. Embassy compound in Baghdad, the embassy urged Americans to leave Iraq (NPR). U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pledged this morning to “keep advancing” with “no mercy for our enemies” (Times of Israel). The U.S. military buildup in the region continues, with the United States deploying additional warships and thousands of marines to the Middle East, multiple news outlets reported (NYT; WSJ). U.S. strikes on Kharg Island—home to a major Iranian oil export terminal—hit military targets, but failed to break the country’s blockade of the waterway, prompting Trump to threaten to target the island’s oil infrastructure if Iran does not fully reopen the strait (Truth Social). Israel issued an evacuation order for parts of Tehran, while Turkey announced its NATO air defenses shot down an incoming Iranian missile, the third in two weeks (IDF; Turkey MoND). Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian oil that was already at sea, saying that the war in Iran should not distract from support for Ukraine (German Chancellor). Iran’s new Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, issued his first public statement since being appointed to the position, demanding the immediate closure of all U.S. military bases in the Middle East; the statement, read out on Iranian state television by a presenter, insisted the Strait of Hormuz must remain closed as leverage against enemies (CBC). State media also reported that Mojtaba Khamenei praised Hezbollah for aiding Iran (NYT). Meanwhile, the Israel Defense Forces announced that it recently struck the Taleghan compound near Tehran, an Iranian nuclear facility allegedly used to develop advanced explosives and conduct sensitive experiments; the site was previously hit in October 2024 and recently targeted again after Israel detected Iran had begun rebuilding it (Times of Israel). In Iraq, a French service member was killed after a pro-Iranian group said it would target French forces (French President). At least four U.S. soldiers died in a plane crash in Iraq that U.S. Central Command said was not due to hostile or friendly fire; that event is still under investigation (CENTCOM). Additionally, Iran intensified its retaliatory attacks, setting fire to two tankers at an Iraqi port after the vessels were struck by suspected Iranian explosive-laden boats (Reuters). The incident prompted Iraqi authorities to suspend all oil terminal operations (NYT). This comes as the price of Brent crude oil sits at around $97.40 a barrel, after it climbed above $100 a barrel earlier in the day (BBC). Despite Trump claiming yesterday that “the straits are in great shape,” the IEA warned today that the war is causing “the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market” (IEA). Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the U.S. Navy is not currently ready to escort tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, adding that such an operation is more likely to happen toward the end of the month (CNBC). While Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations argued that Tehran would not fully close the Strait of Hormuz, the country’s semi-official Fars News Agency said ships passing through “could be at risk from missiles or rogue drones” (Reuters; Bloomberg). In response to the near-halt in oil shipping through the strait and to increase the amount of oil on global markets, the United States temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian oil that was already at sea (NYT). In what appears to be one of the deadliest civilian casualty events in recent U.S. military history, the United States struck an Iranian elementary school on the first day of the war, the New York Times reported based on preliminary findings from a U.S. military investigation (NYT). At least 175 people were killed, according to Iranian state media (WaPo). Outdated targeting information appears to have led the United States to launch a Tomahawk missile at the school, multiple outlets reported (CNN). Asked for comment, the White House press secretary said the investigation was still ongoing (AP). U.S. President Donald Trump, who previously blamed Iran for the strike, said he did not know about the preliminary findings (NBC). His administration has slashed 90 percent of the Pentagon teams responsible for reducing civilian casualties in military operations (NPR). Reports suggest more than 1,300 people have died in Iran, at least 570 in Lebanon, and 15 in Israel, the World Health Organization said (WHO). At least twelve additional people have been killed across Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, according to officials in those countries (NYT). Meanwhile, CBS News reported that dozens of U.S. troops wounded by Iranian drones in Kuwait at the start of the war remain hospitalized with injuries such as brain trauma, shrapnel wounds, and burns (CBS). Meanwhile, Iranian military activity expanded as projectiles struck three vessels, including the Thai-flagged Mayuree Naree dry bulk carrier, near the Strait of Hormuz; in a statement carried by Tasnim News Agency, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed responsibility for the attack (Reuters). At the same time, Iranian forces launched drones and missiles at targets across the Gulf, including a U.S. military base in Kuwait, while Israeli officials reported that Iran fired cluster-munition warheads toward Israel (Al Jazeera; NYT). Gulf governments responded by placing civilians on alert, with authorities in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Saudi Arabia urging residents to seek shelter as air defenses intercepted incoming attacks (CNN). Separately, after a strike damaged a building linked to one of Iran’s largest public banks in Tehran, Iranian officials warned they could target American and Israeli economic and banking interests across the region (Reuters). The UN Security Council condemned Iran’s “egregious attacks” against its neighbors and demanded they stop; it marked the body’s first resolution related to the war and passed by a vote of thirteen to zero, with Russia and China abstaining (UN). While Trump told Axios the war would end “soon,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian wrote on social media it would only end by “recognizing Iran’s legitimate rights, payment of reparations, and firm [international] guarantees against future aggression” (Axios; Iranian President). An Iranian military spokesperson also cautioned that continued destabilization of regional security could push global oil prices to $200 per barrel (Reuters). Amid these threats and rising oil prices, the International Energy Agency announced that member states will release four hundred million barrels of oil from emergency reserves, the largest coordinated release in the agency’s history (WSJ). U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth warned that Tuesday would be the most intense day yet for U.S. strikes on Iran, pledging to deploy the greatest number of fighters and bombers of the campaign (NYT). Meanwhile, the United States deployed a Patriot air defense system to Turkey’s Malatya province, home to a key NATO radar base, as the alliance bolstered its defenses against Iranian missile threats (Reuters). Retaliatory attacks in the region as Iran fired nine ballistic missiles and thirty-five drones at the United Arab Emirates with eight missiles intercepted and one falling into the Persian Gulf; nine drones evaded air defenses and struck inside the country (Times of Israel). Due to the drone strikes, oil company ADNOC closed its Ruwais refinery in the UAE after a fire broke out (Reuters). In Israel, the Israel Defense Forces detected a ballistic missile launch from Iran targeting northern and central regions, while an earlier missile attack on central Israel produced no reported injuries or direct impacts (Times of Israel). Meanwhile, as oil and gas prices continue to rise, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Ali Mohammad Naeini vowed to block all regional oil exports to hostile nations and their partners, dismissing Western efforts to control energy prices as temporary and futile (NYT). Moreover, Iran’s Supreme National Security Council secretary Ali Larijani responded to U.S. President Donald Trump’s threat to strike Iran “twenty times harder” over the Strait of Hormuz blockade, telling the American government to “beware, lest you are the ones who are eliminated,” dismissing the warnings as hollow threats that the Iranian people do not fear (NBC). Amid an international increase in oil prices caused by the effects of Iranian military operations on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the G7 countries have declined to jointly tap their oil reserves to ease costs (Washington Post). The announcement came after the price-per-barrel fell slightly over the weekend in light of reporting that the body was considering such a move (Financial Times). Due to high global energy prices, Bangladesh is closing universities early for the summer; Pakistan and the Philippines both declared a four-day work week (Reuters; Indian Express). The head of Saudi Arabia’s state oil company said that although it will reroute some exports through the Red Sea, continued war would yield “drastic” effects on the world economy (Financial Times). International Monetary Fund chief Kristalina Georgieva said that every ten percent increase in energy prices over the course of 2026 is expected to increase global inflation by almost half a percent (IMF). U.S. President Donald Trump said the war could be over “soon” and that the United States had already achieved many of its military objectives in Iran (White House). However, Trump threatened to escalate if Iranian officials maintain restrictions on oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has pledged to do (Reuters). A top Iranian foreign policy official said the country can keep fighting and sees no room for diplomacy (CNN). Russian President Vladimir Putin congratulated Mojtaba Khamenei on his selection as Iran's new supreme leader (Kremlin). Australia granted humanitarian visas to five Iranian female soccer players; Iranian state television announcer called the women and their teammates “wartime traitors” after they declined to sing the country’s national anthem before a match at the Asian Cup (X; The Athletic). U.S. Central Command announced it has hit more than five thousand Iranian targets and damaged or destroyed more than fifty Iranian ships in ten days of war (X). Turkey said NATO air defenses shot down an incoming Iranian missile in its airspace yesterday for the second time this month (NYT). To help protect Cyprus, which was hit by an Iranian drone last week, the French Navy will send eight frigates and two amphibious assault ships to the Middle East in addition to its current aircraft carrier in the region; the Netherlands will send a naval frigate to the Mediterranean at France’s request; and Turkey deployed six F-16 fighter jets and air defense systems to northern Cyprus (USNI; Reuters; Yahoo). Iran's Assembly of Experts announced Mojtaba Khamenei, 56, as the country's new supreme leader; Khamenei succeeds his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in an Israeli airstrike coordinated with U.S. forces on February 28 (NBC). Earlier in March, U.S. President Donald Trump has called Mojtaba Khamenei an “unacceptable” choice for the new leader of Iran (Axios). While not ruling out future U.S. ground troops in Iran, Trump told reporters that the United States discouraged Kurdish armed groups from entering the war against Iran despite their offer to do so (Anadolu). Newly released footage indicates casualties at an Iranian elementary school on February 28 were caused by a U.S. airstrike targeting an adjacent naval base (NYT). Oil companies in Iraq, Kuwait, and Qatar have begun reducing oil production (WSJ). International shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains largely halted due to Iranian military actions (WSJ). Trump argued on social media that short-term oil prices “will drop rapidly when the destruction of the Iran nuclear threat is over” (Truth Social). Trump and UK Prime Minister Kier Starmer discussed the Iran war on a phone call; Starmer offered to send British aircraft carriers to the Middle East, an offer Trump declined and criticized for coming too late in the conflict (BBC). Some U.S. aircraft have been permitted to land at UK bases in the region on the understanding they will only be used for defensive operations (The Guardian). Water desalination plants were attacked in Iran and Bahrain, officials from both countries said; Iran accused the United States of targeting its infrastructure, a claim that U.S. Central Command denies (NYT). On Saturday, Israel attacked multiple oil facilities in Iran, sparking a fire that blanketed Tehran in black smoke and prompted the Iranian Red Crescent Society to warn of acid rain exposure (Financial Times). The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) announced a new wave of strikes against Iranian regime targets in Tehran and Isfahan (Times of Israel). The IDF also carried out further strikes in the southern suburbs of Beirut, Lebanon (NPR). The Israeli Air Force destroyed the bunker of Iran’s former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, dropping approximately one hundred bombs on the bunker site (Times of Israel). Iranian state media reported that the Iranian Revolutionary Guards sent a wave of missiles and drone toward Tel Aviv, Israel (NYT). In the Gulf, both Kuwait and Bahrain reported damage from Iranian drone and missile strikes (Euronews). Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar reported intercepting Iranian missiles and drones (CNN). Qatar's energy minister warned that Gulf states would likely shut down production, increasing global energy prices, in light of an Iranian strike that damaged Qatar's largest natural gas plant and the ongoing Iranian targeting of oil tankers traveling through the Hormuz Strait (Financial Times). Across the Middle East, at least 230,000 people have been displaced in relation to the ongoing war, according to the UN (Reuters). Iran’s daily missile launches have dropped overall since earlier in March, with U.S. and Israeli forces saying they have degraded many of Iran's missile sites; Iran's military is increasingly carrying out regional attacks using drones (WSJ). Russia is providing intelligence and information that is allowing Iran to target U.S. forces across the Middle East (Washington Post). Iran's foreign minister confirmed Russia is helping Iran's war effort but did not confirm details (NBC). U.S. defense contractors are due to meet with administration officials at the White House today to discuss ramping up weapons production (Reuters). At NATO, there has been no talk of triggering the alliance's Article V mutual defense clause following a recent Iranian attempt to target Turkey with a ballistic missile; NATO intercepted the missile and the Iran Revolutionary Guard Corps denies firing missiles at Turkish territory (Reuters). However, NATO increased its alliance-wide ballistic missile defense posture (X). The Israel Defense Forces continued to strike Iran’s ballistic missile infrastructure, while the United States and Israel moved to target Iranian defense industrial assets (ISW). Azerbaijan reported an Iranian drone strike in Nakhchivan exclave, a claim Iran denies (Axios). The U.S. embassy in Kuwait shut down operations amid missile attacks, while the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Iraq, and Qatar, also reported Iranian missile and drone attacks (AP). Sources report that China is in talks with Iran over oil and gas transit through the Strait of Hormuz (Reuters). U.S. President Donald Trump said he should be personally involved in choosing Iran’s next supreme leader after Ali Khamenei’s death, rejecting likely successor Mojtaba Khamenei as “unacceptable;” Iran continues to delay announcing a new supreme leader (Axios). Trump also called on the Kurdish opposition to support the U.S. war effort and offered air support for their efforts to take territory in western Iran (Washington Post). Asked if Americans should worry about Iranian strikes against the U.S. homeland, Trump told reporters "“I guess. . . . When you go to war, some people will die" (TIME). According to European and Middle Eastern officials briefed on the matter, the current Iranian regime's grip on power is secure (Washington Post). Europol warned Europeans of an increased risk for terrorist activity, cyber attacks, and online radicalization efforts as the war continues (Reuters). Iran's foreign minister told NBC his country is prepared to resist a potential U.S. ground invasion and that Iran is not currently willing to negotiate for a ceasefire (NBC). The United States and its partners in the Middle East have sought Ukraine's expertise and advice on countering Iranian drone operations, which Ukraine is now providing (Washington Post). France has authorized U.S. use of air bases in the country for operations in the Middle East (Reuters). Spain has denied U.S. requests for similar access and cooperation (The Hill). U.S. military officials believe it is likely that U.S. forces were responsible for Saturday’s strike on a girl’s school in Iran (Reuters). Retaliatory strikes by Iran continued as a ballistic missile from Iran was heading towards Turkish airspace; NATO air and missile defenses shot the missile down (NYT). Though it remains unclear where the missile was intended to land, a NATO spokesperson stated that the trans-Atlantic alliance condemned Iran’s targeting of Turkey (Reuters). Iranian missile attacks also targeted three bases in Iraq that were used by Kurdish militant groups that oppose Iran; the Kurdish Freedom Party confirmed the strikes (NYT). In Washington, U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told reporters this morning the United States was “accelerating, not decelerating” military action and said that, alongside Israel, it aimed to gain “uncontested control” of Iranian air (NYT). General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said that Iranian ballistic missile strikes have decreased by 86 percent compared to the first day of fighting and that drone attacks have similarly decreased by 73 percent (NYT). Separately, Hegseth announced that the U.S. military sank an Iranian warship with a torpedo off the coast of Sri Lanka (BBC). Sri Lankan authorities said they rescued thirty-two people on board and recovered multiple bodies; sources from Sri Lanka’s defense ministry and Navy say roughly a hundred others are missing (Reuters). A set of satellite images reviewed by the BBC also shows that U.S. and Israeli strikes destroyed or damaged at least eleven Iranian naval vessels; several missile bases and nuclear sites were also damaged in the attacks (BBC). Meanwhile, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) launched a new wave of strikes targeting Iranian regime members; Kurdish media also reported the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps headquarters being targeted in northwest Iran (Guardian). The IDF also announced a new wave of strikes in southern Lebanon, telling residents to evacuate to the north of the Litani River (Reuters). The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz remains volatile, as at least two hundred vessels, including oil tankers and cargo ships, remain anchored (Reuters). Trump notified Congress in a letter this week that the operations were meant to protect the U.S. homeland and forces in the region, advance U.S. national interests, and ensure “collective self-defense of our regional allies, including Israel” (NYT). Despite U.S. officials’ arguments that an Iranian threat was imminent, the UN nuclear chief said that Iran was not days or weeks away from having a nuclear weapon (CNN). U.S. Central Command stated that the United States has struck over 1,700 targets across Iran, including naval ships, submarines, anti-ship missile sites, and command and control centers (Jerusalem Post). Iranian news agencies also reported that Mehrabad airport was struck soon after the Israel Defense Forces warned civilians near Tehran to evacuate (Reuters). Air attacks further destroyed the building of Iran’s Assembly of Experts in Qom, which is tasked with electing Iran’s new supreme leader (Reuters). The Israel Defense Forces reported that strikes also killed Daoud Ali Zadeh, the acting commander of the Lebanon Corps of the elite Quds Force, in Tehran (AP). Iran launched retaliatory attacks on the U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait (AP; Kuwait MoFA). The State Department urged Americans to leave the Middle East due to “serious safety risks” (State). Despite the U.S. government’s warning urging Americans to leave the region, many airports have been forced to delay or cancel flights because of the conflict (Guardian). Iran also struck energy facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar and fired upon ships in the Strait of Hormuz (AP). Energy markets remain volatile, with European natural gas prices surging at least 40 percent today after Qatar paused exports from a gas facility following the Iranian attack (Bloomberg). U.S. President Donald Trump announced the United States Development Finance Corporation will offer insurance “at a very reasonable price” to ensure maritime trade flows in the Gulf (Truth Social). France and the United Kingdom (UK) announced they would each deploy a warship to the Mediterranean (France 24; BBC).  Plans for new leadership in Iran also remain unclear as Trump told White House reporters that the leaders the administration had in mind are dead, and that an additional group “may be dead also” (AP). According to Iranian media, the commander of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards announced that the Strait of Hormuz is now closed and Iran will fire upon any ship that attempts to pass through (Reuters). Meanwhile, Kuwaiti air defenses mistakenly shot down three American jets during combat operations; U.S. Central Command said in a statement that all six crew members are safe (NYT). U.S. Central Command also raised the U.S. death toll from Operation Epic Fury to four; the fourth servicemember was severely wounded in a Saturday attack on a U.S. base in Kuwait and later succumbed to injuries (CENTCOM). Despite Trump calling on Iranians this weekend to rise up against the regime, top administration officials argued that U.S. aims were focused on degrading Iran’s military capabilities—including its ballistic missiles, navy, and security infrastructure (White House; Pentagon). Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth framed the U.S.-Israeli strikes that killed Khamenei as “not a so-called regime change war,” but quickly added “the regime sure did change” (NPR). Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have both encouraged Iranians to rise up against the remnants of the regime (AP).  The White House said in a statement that Trump’s “unequivocal” demand remains that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon (White House). Trump wrote in a social media post last night that U.S. munitions stockpiles remain high and “Wars can be fought ‘forever’” (Truth Social). Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine said the attacks had taken “months, and in some cases, years” of planning with the goal of stopping Tehran’s “ability to project power outside of its borders” (France24). Although Trump told reporters yesterday that Iran had indicated interest in resuming talks, Iran’s top national security official, Ali Larijani, wrote on social media today that Iran would not negotiate with the United States (X). Secretary of State Marco Rubio caused a stir when he told reporters that the U.S. attack on Iran was in part driven by Israel’s plans to strike Iran; because Iran would have retaliated by attacking U.S. forces, a preemptive U.S. attack was necessary, Rubio said (State). While many congressional Republicans praised the U.S. military campaign, leading Democrats condemned it as illegal and reckless and vowed to vote on a resolution restricting Trump’s war powers (NPR). The death toll continues to rise: the Iranian Red Crescent reported at least 555 people have been killed in Iran, while 11 people have been killed in Israel (AP). U.S. Central Command announced in a statement that three U.S. service members were killed and five others were seriously wounded in yesterday’s attack on Iran; President Trump said there would “likely be more” U.S. casualties (CENTCOM; White House). Operations continued as CENTCOM stated that a large-scale U.S. strike destroyed the IRGC headquarters (CENTCOM). Satellite imagery also shows damage to Iran’s naval and air bases, while President Trump stated that the operations sank nine Iranian naval ships (NPR; Truth Social). Trump has given varying estimates of how long U.S. military engagement could last, telling different media outlets over the weekend it could be days or up to 4 to 5 weeks (NYT). Speaking to The Atlantic, Trump appeared to float an off-ramp, suggesting that he would be willing to speak with Iran’s new leadership (The Atlantic). Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on social media that Trump had launched the war despite a new nuclear deal being “within reach” (X). Meanwhile, Israel announced it launched another round of strikes “in the heart of Iran” (CNN). Retaliatory strikes from Iran also continued, as an Iranian missile strike in Beit Shamesh killed nine Israeli citizens (NYT). Three people were also killed in the United Arab Emirates, while Kuwait’s Health Ministry reported one death from the retaliatory strikes (Jerusalem Post). Six nearby countries condemned Iran’s retaliatory strikes across the region (Saudi Press Agency). Videos and images verified by the New York Times indicate yesterday’s bombing of an elementary school in southern Iran killed at least 175 people (NYT). Oil shipping traffic slowed to a near stop in the Strait of Hormuz, while a key international oil price jumped at least 8 percent (Bloomberg). The United States and Israel announced that they had initiated a large-scale military operation designed to destroy Iran’s military capabilities and bring about regime change (Axios). The commander of the U.S. Central Command said the operation began at 1:15 a.m. ET and targeted aspects of Iran’s security apparatus that posed an imminent threat (CENTCOM). The operation, named “Operation Epic Fury” by the United States, utilized Tomahawk missiles, F-18 and F-35 fighter jets, and, for the first time, single-use drones (Reuters). The combined U.S.-Israel force conducted close to nine hundred strikes, as the Israel Defense Forces claimed it had struck at least five hundred Iranian targets (ISW). Iranian state media confirmed that Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the attacks; Iranian Defense Minister Amir Nasirzadeh and Revolutionary Guards commander Mohammed Pakpour were also reportedly killed alongside five other senior military commanders (Reuters). Iranian state media also reported that Khamenei’s daughter, grandchild, daughter-in-law, and son-in-law were killed in the attacks (Times of Israel). The U.S.-Israel operations triggered a retaliatory campaign by Iran as Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates faced Iranian missiles, drones, and intercepts (Axios). At least one U.S. military installation in Bahrain, which headquarters the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, was struck by Iranian missile fire; Iranian state media reported that missile attacks also targeted Ali al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait, al-Udeid Air Base in Qatar, and al-Dhafra Air Base in the United Arab Emirates among other non-military sites, including luxury hotels and residential buildings in Bahrain and Dubai (WaPo). UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for immediate de-escalation at an emergency Security Council meeting Saturday, condemning the United States and Israel’s strikes as unlawful (AP). Both countries argued their actions were justified given the major nature of the threat posed by Iran, while Iran said it posed no imminent threat (UN). As the United States weighs a strike on Iran, it authorized non-essential government staff and family members to depart Israel, citing unspecified “safety risks” (U.S. Embassy Jerusalem). China also urged its citizens in Iran to evacuate as soon as possible (Reuters). The threat of renewed conflict comes as Israel’s stockpiles of ground-based ballistic missile interceptors and U.S. land- and sea-based antiballistic missile systems, both used extensively during the June 2025 Iran–Israel conflict, were significantly depleted, raising concerns about the sustainability of Israel’s air defense coverage in the event of another exchange (NYT). Separately, the International Atomic Energy Agency reported that some of Iran’s uranium enriched to up to 60 percent purity, near weapons grade, is stored in an underground tunnel complex at its Isfahan nuclear site, which appears largely undamaged despite U.S. and Israeli strikes that hit the facility’s entrance in June (Reuters). The United States and Iran held another round of indirect nuclear talks today in Geneva, with both sides threatening war if diplomacy fails (BBC). The countries are floating proposals that include limiting the amount of uranium Iran is allowed to enrich, temporarily suspending Iran’s enrichment activity, and dismantling its main nuclear sites, according to reports from multiple news outlets (Guardian). Both sides agreed to resume negotiations within a week, with additional technical-level discussions scheduled in Vienna (Reuters). The state news agency of mediator Oman said today that both sides were demonstrating “unprecedented openness to new and creative ideas and solutions” (Oman News Agency). Further, the foreign minister of Oman said the talks had achieved “significant progress,” but did not announce a breakthrough that would avert an attack (Oman FM).

title: Sweden ‘open’ to NATO role in reopening Strait of Hormuz - politico.eu
content: Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard said NATO allies would discuss the issue at a high-level meeting Friday. HELSINGBORG, Sweden — Stockholm is leaving the door open to a possible role for NATO in reopening the critical Strait of Hormuz waterway, Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard told POLITICO. “It's definitely in Swedish and European interests to make sure that we keep the strait open and that Iran cannot use this as a weapon again,” she said in an interview ahead of Friday's meeting of NATO foreign ministers. “So I'm quite open to discussing different formats.” Tehran brought commercial traffic to a standstill in retaliation for the U.S.-Israeli bombing campaign against Iran that began on Feb. 28. But NATO has largely stayed out of talks on restoring normal traffic through the trade chokepoint — responsible for about a fifth of the world's oil shipments — amid disagreements over the war, with some European countries like France, Spain, Italy and the U.K. restricting U.S. access to their airspace or bases. In response, U.S. President Donald Trump branded NATO a “paper tiger” and warned of reprisals. Earlier this month, he announced a cut of 5,000 troops from Germany over comments criticizing the war by the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz. A loose coalition of around 40 countries led by France and the U.K. has instead become the central forum for efforts to reopen the strait, but only on condition that hostilities end. However, some NATO countries would prefer the alliance take on a more formal role that either takes over from the coalition or launches its own mission, said two NATO diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely about a sensitive topic. They said that could also help showcase the value of the alliance to Trump, who has repeatedly raised doubts over U.S. commitment to NATO. “That will definitely be discussed during this meeting,” Stenergard said in the southern Swedish city of Helsingborg. While NATO should “always be careful to create new precedents” in considering a possible role in the Middle East, she added, “it's very important that we make sure that we protect the freedom of navigation because it is fundamental for free trade.” Other allies are similarly warming to the idea of a NATO role. “I think it's always important that we do things in a coordinated way,” Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen told reporters in Helsingborg on Friday. “We need the expertise of NATO there as well.” But an alliance-led operation would require consensus among its 32 members — and some allies are still drawing a red line against any involvement. NATO’s “North Atlantic Treaty applies to the North Atlantic region,” French foreign ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux told POLITICO, “and it is not its purpose nor is it the right alliance to focus on the issue in the Middle East and the Strait of Hormuz.” Invite comes despite U.S. resisting efforts to extend invitations to non-NATO leaders. Warsaw hailed the move as proof Poland remains Washington’s “ironclad ally.” Mark Rutte wants new focus on defense industry deals to close a yawning production gap in Europe — but also keep the U.S. president on board. Even Berlin is now reconsidering its opposition to punitive measures against Israeli officials.

title: US and Iran narrow gaps but nuclear stockpile, Hormuz still sticking points - The Arab Weekly
content: This website uses cookies to ensure you get the best experience on our website The US and Iran stuck to opposed stances on Thursday over Tehran’s uranium stockpile and control on the Strait of Hormuz, although US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had been “some good signs” in talks. US President Donald Trump said the US will eventually recover Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, which Washington believes is destined for a nuclear weapon. “We will get it. We don’t need it, we don’t want it. We’ll probably destroy it after we get it, but we’re not going to let them have it,” Trump told reporters at the White House. Meanwhile, Iran’s Supreme Leader has issued a directive that the country’s near-weapons-grade uranium should not be sent abroad, senior Iranian sources told Reuters, hardening Tehran’s stance on one of the main US demands at peace talks. Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei’s order could complicate talks on ending the war. Israeli officials have said that Trump has assured Israel that Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, needed to make an atomic weapon, will be sent out of Iran and that any peace deal must include a clause on this. Israeli Prime Minister Binyamin Netanyahu has said he will not consider the war over until enriched uranium is removed from Iran, Tehran ends its support for proxy militias, and its ballistic missile capabilities are eliminated. But Iran’s top officials believe that sending the material abroad would leave the country more vulnerable to future attacks by the United States and Israel. Before the war, Iran signalled willingness to ship out half of its stockpile of uranium which has been enriched to 60%, a level far higher than what is needed for civilian uses. But sources said that position changed after repeated threats from Trump to strike Iran. Some in Tehran believe there are “feasible formulas” to resolve the matter. “There are solutions like diluting the stockpile under the supervision of the International Atomic Energy Agency,” an Iranian source told Reuters. A second contentious issue in the talks is that of access to the Strait of Hormuz, where Teheran is jockeying to impose long-term control. “The regime is trying to establish a new reality born from a clear military defeat, but attempts to control the Strait of Hormuz or infringe on the UAE’s maritime sovereignty are nothing but pipe dreams,” said the United Arab Emirates’ presidential adviser Anwar Gargash in a post on X. Iran’s new body overseeing the Strait of Hormuz said its claimed area of control extends to Emirati waters, drawing a sharp rebuke from the Gulf neighbour. Trump also railed against Iran’s intentions to charge fees for use of the strait, where a fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas transited before the war. “We want it open, we want it free. We don’t want tolls,” he said. “It’s an international waterway.” Iran’s deputy foreign minister on Thursday restated Tehran’s claims to “sovereignty” over the strait. Some ships are managing to transit the  strait, but only a trickle compared with the 125-140 daily passages before the war. Rubio told reporters a diplomatic solution would be unfeasible if Tehran implemented a tolling system in the Strait of Hormuz. But he added that there had been some progress in talks. “There’s some good signs,” Rubio said. “I don’t want to be overly optimistic … So, let’s see what happens over the next few days.” A senior Iranian source said on Thursday that no deal has been reached but that gaps have been narrowed. Trump has said he is ready to resume strikes on Iran if he does not get the “right answers” from Iran’s leadership. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards have warned that renewed attacks would trigger retaliation beyond its region. Pakistani Interior Minister Syed Mohsin Naqvi on Wednesday made his second trip to Tehran this week, carrying a message from the United States, and held talks with Iranian leaders. “We’re speaking to all the various groups in Iran to streamline communication and so things pick up pace,” said one of the sources familiar with negotiations. “Trump’s patience running thin is a concern, but we’re working on the pace at which messages are relayed from each side.” Tehran submitted its latest offer to the US this week. Tehran’s descriptions suggest it largely repeats terms Trump previously rejected, including demands for control of the Strait of Hormuz, compensation for war damage, lifting of sanctions, release of frozen assets and the withdrawal of US troops. Trump and Netanyahu said their war aims were to curb Iran’s support for regional militias, dismantle its nuclear programme, destroy its missile capabilities and make it easier for Iranians to topple their rulers. But Iran has so far retained its stockpile of near-weapons-grade enriched uranium, and its ability to threaten neighbours with missiles, drones and proxy militias. It has also maintained tight control over the population at home.

title: First Oil Tanker to Exit Hormuz since War Expected in Japan - Rigzone
content:
Japan - one of Asia’s biggest importers of energy from the Middle East - flagged the impending arrival of the first Persian Gulf oil shipment to transit the contested Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began. The Idemitsu Maru, a very large crude carrier that passed through the waterway in late April, could dock as soon as Monday, according to the trade ministry. Hauling 2 million barrels of Saudi crude, the vessel is on track to arrive at Idemitsu Kosan Co.'s Aichi refinery, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry said in a briefing document on Friday. The war in the Middle East has led to the near-total closure of the maritime chokepoint, triggering an unprecedented energy supply shock and prompting mainstay importers across Asia to scour the globe for alternative crude and natural gas shipments. Along with other developed nations, Japan also moved to tap strategic reserves to cushion itself from the impact of the conflict. While a handful of vessels have managed to navigate Hormuz, the overall tally of daily passages remains at a fraction of the pre-war total. Tehran is discussing with Oman how to set up a toll system to formalize its control of the conduit, the Iranian ambassador to France told Bloomberg this week. A second Japan-linked tanker, the Eneos Endeavor, also crossed the chokepoint earlier in May. The Eneos Endeavor was not mentioned in the briefing. What do you think?
